To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the minor group binding protein of human rhinovirus type 14 is a cell surface glycoprotein that is shed into the medium in a Ca(2+) dependent manner and that the intracellular pool of the receptor is sufficient to restore the cell surface receptor activity after trypsin stripping of the cells.

the rhinovirus binding protein, which is anchored to the membrane by a glycosylphosphatidylinositol linkage, can be released into the medium from the cell surface by a process that is dependent on Ca2+.
a soluble rhinovirus binding protein is released by a Ca(2+)dependent proteolytic mechanism from the surface of HeLa cells.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the release of a rhinivrus-binding protein into the medium of infected HeLa cells.
the shedding of the rhinovirus 1B binding protein from the cell surface and its potential involvement in virus-cell interaction.
a possible mechanism for the shedding of rhinovirus binding proteins.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the rhinovirus receptor is not a stable protein, and that the shedding of the virus-binding activity may represent a mechanism for the regulation of rhinovirus infection.
the shedding of the minor group receptor is a calcium-dependent, proteolytic process, which is not necessarily linked to a decrease in virus binding.
the shedding of the minor group rhinovirus binding protein from the surface of HeLa cells is a Ca2+-dependent process which does not affect virus binding to the cells.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the rhinovirus binding site on HeLa cells is a protein of M(r) 85,000 that is shed from the cell surface by a Ca(2+) dependent process.
the virus binding protein is a Ca(2+) dependent protein that is released from the membrane by a protease or a phospholipases.
the rhinovirus receptor is not a stable component of the cell surface and that the receptor shedding is a reversible process.
The main takeaway from our work is that
rhinovirus binding proteins are shed from the cell surface, and the process is Ca2+-dependent.
the rhinovirus receptor can be released from the cell surface by Ca(2+).
shedding is a regulated process that occurs on a timescale of hours and is not simply due to passive diffusion.
